## Why the Sky Is Blue

Sunlight contains all the colors of the visible spectrum, but as it passes through Earth's atmosphere, it collides with gas molecules (primarily nitrogen and oxygen). These molecules scatter the incoming light, and—crucially—they scatter shorter wavelengths far more effectively than longer ones. Because blue and violet light have the shortest wavelengths in the visible spectrum, they get scattered in all directions across the sky, reaching our eyes from every angle and giving the sky its characteristic blue color. (The reason we see blue rather than violet is that our eyes are more sensitive to blue, sunlight contains more blue than violet, and some violet is absorbed higher in the atmosphere.)

## Rayleigh Scattering Wavelength Dependence

The intensity of light scattered by particles much smaller than the wavelength follows an inverse fourth-power relationship:

$$I \propto \frac{1}{\lambda^4}$$

This means that halving the wavelength increases the scattered intensity by a factor of $2^4 = 16$. This strong wavelength dependence is exactly why blue light (~450 nm) scatters roughly $(700/450)^4 \approx 6$ times more than red light (~700 nm), which is the physical basis for the blue sky.
